summary: Costa Rica grants visa-free stays of up to 180 days to citizens of the US, Canada, the UK, the EU, Australia, Japan and many other countries, strictly expects proof of onward travel (airlines enforce it at check-in), and lets many visa-required nationals enter with a valid US, Canadian or Schengen visa instead of a Costa Rican consular visa.

conditionalWaivers.text: Visa-required nationals holding a valid multiple-entry US or Canadian visa (not C1, C2 or C3 transit visas) or US or Canadian residence, a multiple-entry Schengen C or D visa, or a residence permit from the UK, the EU, Iceland, Norway or Switzerland valid at least 90 more days, may enter Costa Rica without a Costa Rican visa for up to 30 days, never beyond the visa's expiry.

fee.notes: Consular tariff for a visa the consulate grants. A visa that needs authorization from the Dirección General de Migración y Extranjería, the route for restricted nationalities, costs USD 50, and a multiple-entry visa it authorizes USD 100. Restricted nationalities also wait longer for that authorization.

passportValidity.text: Depends on nationality. First-group nationalities (including the US, Canada, the UK, the EU, Australia and Japan) need a passport valid on the day of entry, but you will not be given more days than the passport has left. Second-group nationalities need 90 days' validity, and nationalities that need a visa need 180 days. Airlines may apply stricter checks of their own.

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever vaccination certificate (ICVP) is required if you have been, in the six days before arrival, in a country on Costa Rica's risk list: Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, French Guiana, Guyana, Paraguay, Peru, Suriname, Trinidad and Tobago and Venezuela in the Americas, and 27 African countries, among them Angola, Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda and Zambia. The vaccine must be given at least 10 days before entry. Direct arrivals from North America or Europe are not affected.

travelInsurance.text: Travel insurance is no longer an entry requirement (the COVID-era insurance mandate ended). Medical coverage is still recommended — private hospitals are excellent but expensive.

onwardTicket.text: Proof of onward or return travel leaving Costa Rica within your permitted stay is a legal entry requirement, and airlines enforce it strictly at check-in, refusing boarding without it. A bus ticket out of the country also counts, but a confirmed flight is safest.

source.name: Dirección General de Migración y Extranjería — Directrices Generales de Visas de Ingreso y Permanencia para No Residentes (November 2025)

proofOfFunds.text: Proof of economic means is a legal entry requirement: at least USD 100 for each month or part of a month of your stay. Most tourists are never asked, but carry a bank card or recent statement.

currencyLimits.text: Cash, traveller's cheques or goods worth USD 10,000 or more must be declared on arrival. Keep the certified declaration: without it, the money can be seized when you leave.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Costa Rica travel advice: entry requirements

notes: Duty-free allowance: 500 g of tobacco and 5 liters of alcoholic beverages per adult.
Strict biosecurity rules apply to fresh fruit, plants, seeds and animal products. Declare them or leave them at home.
The USD 29 air departure charge (USD 27 tax plus USD 2 baggage scanning) is included in the ticket by most airlines — if yours does not include it, pay it at the airport before check-in.

payments.text: Cards are accepted almost everywhere tourists go, and US dollars are accepted nearly universally (change comes in colones, often at a poor rate). Keep some colones in cash for sodas (small local restaurants), rural areas, buses and tips.

safety.text: Costa Rica is one of the safer countries in Central America, but petty theft is the main visitor risk — never leave belongings visible in a parked rental car or unattended on a beach. Rip currents cause more tourist deaths than crime; swim only at beaches with lifeguards or ask locally about conditions.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Costa Rica travel advice

bestTimeToVisit.text: December to April is the dry season ("verano") on the Pacific side — the most reliable weather for beaches and wildlife; the green season (May–November) is cheaper and lush, with mostly-sunny mornings and afternoon downpours.

tips.text: Book your exit before you fly — airlines strictly enforce Costa Rica's onward-ticket rule at check-in and will refuse boarding on a one-way itinerary without proof of onward travel.

Renting a car? Mandatory local liability insurance is added on top of quoted prices (budget for it), never leave anything in a parked car, and check whether your route needs 4x4 — some beach-town roads involve unbridged river crossings that rental contracts often exclude.
Rip currents are the leading cause of tourist deaths in Costa Rica. Many popular beaches have no lifeguards. If caught, swim parallel to the shore until free of the current, then in.
Tap water is safe to drink in most of Costa Rica, including San José and the main tourist towns; in remote coastal or rural spots, ask locally or use bottled water.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Costa Rica?
faq.answer: No. US citizens enter Costa Rica visa-free for tourism and can be granted up to 180 days. You do need a passport valid for your stay and proof of onward travel — airlines check for the onward ticket before boarding.

faq.question: How long can tourists stay in Costa Rica?
faq.answer: Visa-free nationals of the first group (US, Canada, UK, EU, Japan and many more) can be granted up to 180 days. The immigration officer decides the exact number of days at entry. Check the stamp in your passport, as it controls your legal stay.

faq.question: Can I enter Costa Rica with a US or Schengen visa instead of a Costa Rican visa?
faq.answer: Often yes. Nationals of visa-required countries who hold a valid multiple-entry visa or residence permit for the United States, Canada or the Schengen area can generally enter Costa Rica without a consular visa, for up to 30 days (or until the visa expires, if sooner). Confirm the current rules for your nationality with a Costa Rican consulate before booking.

faq.question: Do I need a yellow fever vaccination for Costa Rica?
faq.answer: Only if you have been, in the six days before arrival, in a country on Costa Rica's yellow fever risk list: Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, French Guiana, Guyana, Paraguay, Peru, Suriname, Trinidad and Tobago, Venezuela and 27 African countries. In that case you must show an ICVP certificate for a vaccine given at least 10 days before entry. Direct arrivals from North America or Europe need nothing.

faq.question: Do I have to pay a departure tax when leaving Costa Rica?
faq.answer: Usually not at the airport. Leaving by air costs USD 29 (a USD 27 exit tax plus a USD 2 baggage-scanning fee), and since 2015 most airlines include it in the ticket; Banco de Costa Rica, which collects the tax, lists the carriers that do. If yours does not, pay it before check-in. Leaving overland costs USD 8 (USD 5 exit tax, USD 2 baggage scanning and USD 1 for the animal-health quarantine service), payable online or at the border.
